
Thank you for submitting your manuscript PA-2025-0186 titled "Tracking Civic Space in Developing Countries with a High-Quality Corpus of Domestic Media and Transformer Models" for consideration.

It has been reviewed and the assigned Associate Editor has read it. The comments of the reviewers and Associate Editor are included at the bottom of this letter.

Based on these reports, we have issued a decision of "reject and resubmit." Here's what that means: we see significant promise in this manuscript, and so would be excited to consider a revision along the lines detailed below. However, a traditional "revise and resubmit" indicates that we believe a paper has at least a 75% chance of acceptance given a good-faith effort to address the issues raised in the review. In this case, the work involved is more substantial, and even if you are able to revise the manuscript in the directions detailed below, the bar to publication is still lofty. So, we are issuing a "reject and resubmit," meaning that we welcome a resubmission but want to acknowledge that the resubmission is no guarantee of future acceptance.

Let us know if you plan to revise. Given the uncertain prospects and the work involved, we of course understand if you choose not to revise, and hope that the reviews are helpful in any event. If you do opt to revise, please upload a clean version of your paper (no tracked changes or comments) in the File Upload step of the resubmission process.
[5:05 PM]Reviewer: 1

Comments to the Author
The article describes an attempt to measure domestic “civic space activity” for a global set of countries using large-scale scraping of news sources and subsequent text analysis. It describes the methodology and the resulting data, conducts a set of validation exercises and presents an applied example predicting onsets of travel restrictions from the new dataset. Overall, this is a very impressive project. The selection of sources is very broad and goes well beyond what existing datasets use. The paper is extremely diligent in analyzing issues that could arise in the data collection (for example, the “false” peak in Zambia), and the execution and write-up is very thorough. If we can push event data coding to the next level using large-scale computational infrastructures and automatic coding, this paper is currently the best and most convincing attempt I have seen to do so. Nevertheless, there is one major issue. Even though the paper relates directly to the many event collections that exist in the discipline (automatic and human coding), it falls short in comparison to these efforts because it does not produce a set of events, but rather approximates “civic space” by the number of articles published about a particular type of activity. This brackets out much of the complexity involved in event coding: the extraction of event-specific information (for example, the political faction(s) involved in a coup) and most importantly, the de-duplication of several reports about the same event into a single instance of this event. For that reason, I am afraid that with its current aim (to produce numbers of articles), the project will be of very limited use to comparative political scientists. Although I do think that the first stage of the project (the systematic scraping of many local news sources) is extremely impressive, to merit publication in PA the project needs to complete the second stage: the compilation of an automatically-coded event dataset. Using cutting-edge LLMs, the processing of these articles should be possible with a high degree of detail, while remaining completely automatic/computational. Once this is done, this project has the potential to replace many of the event collections that currently exist. It is not a recommendation I give easily, but at this point I cannot support publication, and the necessary changes to the entire project are too extensive to recommend revisions.

Reports/events distinction. The paper sets out by reviewing the event coding and analysis literature, which creates the expectation that it does something similar. However, this is not the case. The approach presented in the paper collects articles and filters them when it comes to the event type they describe. However, the literature has recognized that events and the reports about them are distinct (see e.g. Weidmann and Rød, Journal of Peace Research 2015, or Cook and Weidmann, AJPS 2019). This means that articles oftentimes report about multiple events, and individual events are oftentimes covered in several articles by different outlets. If we simply count articles, we may be picking up patterns of reporting rather than actual events on the ground. These patterns may account for some of the findings presented in this paper, for example that most of the coverage comes from domestic sources. This would indeed be an interesting finding if the numbers referred to actual events, but they do not – these numbers simply say that there are more domestic articles than international ones. This is not surprising. Even if article numbers correlate largely with events on the ground – which they probably do – the article numbers produced by this project are not usable for many applications: We cannot infer the number of events from the number of articles, since we do not know how particular events trigger reporting (the relationship is likely not linear, and will differ between event categories and sequences – see for example Hellmeier, Weidmann and Rød, Political Communication 2018). Also, we lack information about the events: who was involved, etc. I believe that these issues can only be resolved if the project separates reports and events explicitly as suggested in the literature, and implements an aggregation procedure by which reports are aggregated to the level of events.

Validation. For a better comparison with existing event data collections, the project needs to implement more thorough validation test. At this point, none of the tests presented in the paper involves an existing event dataset. Of course, this would only be possible for particular types of events included in the project, for example coups. This would help answer the question of whether there are “coups” in the dataset that are not picked up by these existing datasets, or whether the project fails to pick up instances included in these datasets. The validation needs to go further and should answer whether potential discrepancies are due to the project’s focus on local sources (which may, or may not, be more reliable and less biased sources – we don’t know), or due to the automatic coding procedure. This is important to know, from a methodological perspective, but also for the users of the new data.

Procedure. I have several questions about the procedure. What exactly is meant by “aggregation” in Fig. 1? Since the project only deals with articles, how is this done, and why? Also, the “political relevance” (p. 9) needs a lot more explanation. How is “relevance” defined? Relevance in the public discourse? Again, I believe that what the authors mean is relevance due to the involvement of state/government actors. So why not code the perpetrator explicitly (as event coding would do) and then drop those events where the perpetrator is not a state/government actor?



Reviewer: 2

Comments to the Author
This is a very interesting contribution that introduces and describes a potentially very useful dataset for civil society research and beyond. I very much appreciate the authors’ work on creating a high-quality dataset from newspaper data.
Nevertheless, before publication, I think the authors should address a number of points in order to more transparently present their contribution:

1) My first point is mostly stylistic: Reading the abstract and the first couple of pages, I assumed that the article’s contribution would be the ML4P dataset, and that this dataset would build on an already existing news corpus (HQMARC). Only later in the article (on page 5) did I realise that HQMARC is not an external resource that the authors use, but that its collection and the subsequent creation of the ML4P dataset are closely interlinked and that this article essentially also introduces the HQMARC corpus resouce.

2) For both resources, the HQMARC corpus of news reports and the ML4P event dataset, the authors do not clearly state whether and under which conditions they will be made available to other researchers/the general public. Will the collected news data in HQMARC be a publicly accessible resource like the common crawl web scraping data or the common-crawl-news data? Or will only the tools (python scripts or packages) to create the corpus be made available while the data itself has to be recreated by other researchers wanting to use this resource?
In the latter case, this would most likely mean that each crawl will produce different dataset, because websites change, older content will no longer be available. In this case HQMARC would actually be a rather unstable and not so “HQ” resource.
The same goes for ML4P: Where and under which conditions will other researchers be able to access the dataset? Will the dataset be updated in the future or will it be a one-time, stable resource that covers the years 2012-2024?

3) I’m not fully convinced by the authors’ decision to create the ML4P dataset based only on the headline and the first 600 characters of each article. While I understand the reasoning that this serves to filter out potentially less relevant content at the end of an article, this effectively reduces the dataset to those events that only, that are the respective article’s main topic. So if an article reports e.g. about preparations for or outcomes of an election and only later mentions that there have been some protests accompanying this election, these protests would be overlooked.
An alternative approach would be to start with a list of keywords for the relevant civic space categories (as in Appendix B) and then reduce the relevant article text to only those sentences that contain at least one of the relevant keyword (and possible one leading and one trailing sentence). Such an approach would ensure that events of activism, cooperation, legal action, and protest that may often not be an article’s main topic also are represented in the final dataset.

4) The authors report that their fine-tuned RoBerta model reaches 82 % out of sample accuracy. Here I would like to see a more detailed documentation of the model performance: Please report precision, recall and f1 scores for each category and the respective weighted scores. Also, my experience is that binary relevance classifiers usually reach higher scores than multi-label classifiers (and this also seems to be the case here). Would it therefore not be a better idea to change the processing order: first remove irrelevant articles, and then only classify the (potentially) relevant remaining articles. This may lead to a better overall performance of the pipeline.

5) I’m not convinced that the “Forecasting Travel Advisory Onsets” use case really helps the article. The analysis is quite complex and rests on a lot of assumptions that cannot really be discussed in the very limited space available. I think the major event validation already fulfils the purpose of showing the real-world use of the dataset, whereas the use case generates more questions than answers: Of course, it makes sense that the declaration of martial law will correlate with travel warnings, but why should election events predict travel warnings in the longer term? And how good is actually a model with “a ROC-AUC of 0.89, AUC-PR of 0.54, and Brier score of 0.12”?
My advice would be to delete the use case.

6) Under limitations the authors never mention paywalls. While I never worked with data from news outlets in the Global South, in the Global North paywalls are a very serious problem regarding access to the relevant news content. Depending on the media source more or less large parts (and often rather more than less) parts of the reporting are only accessible for paying users. It may be that this is less relevant for the first 600 characters of an article, but I know that many news outlets do not allow access even to the first couple of sentences. So, what does this mean for the selectivity of articles in the HQMARC corpus? Does this differ between countries, and if so, does this have an effect on the reliability of the dataset?

Despite all these questions, I do gratulate the authors to their important work, and I’m very much looking forward to seeing the article and hopefully also the two datasets being published.
[5:06 PM]Associate Editor
Comments to the Author:
Both reviewers note substantial contributions of the paper, especially the dataset. While one reviewer is more positive than the other, both reviewers flag substantial changes that would be needed for publication. In particular, Reviewer 1 questions whether the authors' coding of civic space is useful in comparison to coding events. Here, the authors could address this either by changing the task or by showing more convincingly that their measure of civic space is useful for political science. Both reviewers stress the need for more validation.
